result.markdown:
# Subset Selection

[Slides for this lecture](10-subset-selection_slides.html)



::: {.callout-tip}
### Learning objectives
After this lecture you should be able to

- **define** best subset, forward stepwise, and backward stepwise selection,
**compare** their cost ($2^p$ least squares fits against $1 + p(p+1)/2$), and
**explain** why the stepwise paths need not contain the best model of each
size,
- **explain** why the training RSS and $R^2$ cannot choose the number of
features $d$ in a model,
- **derive** the $2(d + 1)\sigma^2$ optimism of the training RSS from the
covariance between observed and fitted responses, **explain** why $C_p$
estimates the error on new responses at the observed feature values, and
**compute** $C_p$, BIC, and adjusted $R^2$ for least squares models of each
size, stating what each penalizes,
- **carry out** $k$-fold cross-validation of the model size in which the best
model of each size is found inside each fold from the training folds only,
and **compare** the size it chooses with the sizes the criteria choose, and
- **interpret** the coefficients of a selected model, including what a
dropped dummy variable does to the reference level, and **explain** why its
standard errors and $p$-values are optimistic.
:::

## Used car prices

### Data

**Question.** Which of the recorded explanatory variables should a model of a
used car's price use?

**Data.** `modeldata::car_prices` records 804 used
General Motors cars for sale in 2005. The response is the price, `Price`, in
dollars. The explanatory variables are the mileage (`Mileage`), the number of
engine cylinders (`Cylinder`), the number of doors (`Doors`), indicators of
cruise control (`Cruise`), an upgraded sound system (`Sound`), and leather
seats (`Leather`), the make (Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, Pontiac, Saab, or
Saturn), and the body style (convertible, coupe, hatchback, sedan, or wagon).
The data store make and body style as one indicator column per level. The
tabs plot price against mileage, one panel per make, and against each of the
other explanatory variables.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_names <- c("Buick", "Cadillac", "Chevy", "Pontiac", "Saab", "Saturn")
body_names <- c("convertible", "coupe", "hatchback", "sedan", "wagon")
level_of <- function(data, columns) columns[max.col(as.matrix(data[columns]))]
car_data <- modeldata::car_prices |>
  mutate(make = factor(level_of(modeldata::car_prices, make_names), levels = make_names),
         body = factor(level_of(modeldata::car_prices, body_names), levels = body_names))
n <- nrow(car_data)

violin <- geom_violin(fill = "grey90", scale = "width",
                      quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), quantile.linetype = "solid")
mileage_axis <- scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(),
                                   breaks = c(0, 20000, 40000))
mileage_plot <- ggplot(car_data, aes(x = Mileage, y = Price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ make) +
  mileage_axis +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = "Mileage", y = "Price", title = "modeldata::car_prices")

group_levels <- c(make_names, body_names)
group_plot <- bind_rows(
  tibble(variable = "Make", level = as.character(car_data$make), Price = car_data$Price),
  tibble(variable = "Body style", level = as.character(car_data$body), Price = car_data$Price)) |>
  mutate(level = factor(level, levels = group_levels),
         variable = factor(variable, levels = c("Make", "Body style"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = level, y = Price)) +
  violin +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Price", title = "modeldata::car_prices",
       caption = "Lines = quartiles and median.")

option_names <- c("Cylinder", "Doors", "Cruise", "Sound", "Leather")
option_plot <- car_data |>
  mutate(across(c(Cruise, Sound, Leather), \(v) if_else(v == 1, "Yes", "No")),
         across(c(Cylinder, Doors), as.character)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(option_names), names_to = "variable", values_to = "level") |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = option_names)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = level, y = Price)) +
  violin +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Price", title = "modeldata::car_prices",
       caption = "Lines = quartiles and median.")
# Median price at each level of an explanatory variable, for prose.
median_by <- function(v) tapply(car_data$Price, car_data[[v]], median)
```
:::

Within every make, price falls with mileage. Make matters more: every
Cadillac costs more than every Saturn, and Saab prices sit well above those of
Chevrolets and Pontiacs. Convertibles cost the most of the body styles. Cars
with more cylinders or with cruise control tend to cost more. Doors and
leather seats make little difference to the median price on their own:
\$17,631 with two doors against
\$18,073 with four, and
\$17,895 without leather against
\$18,126 with it. Cars with an upgraded sound
system have a lower median price than cars without one,
\$17,161 against
\$20,648; Chevrolets, the
most common make and one of the cheapest, have one
82.8% of the time. Prices
spread more widely where they are higher:
the Cadillac panel spans a far wider range of dollars than the Saturn
panel.

### Candidate features

The first five explanatory variables enter as features as recorded, with
`Cylinder` treated as a number (4, 6, or 8). Make and body style are
categorical explanatory variables, and their indicator columns are complete
sets: every car has exactly one make and one body style, so the six make
indicators sum to 1, the intercept column. Each needs a reference level whose
indicator is left out; here Saturn for make and wagon for body style.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
doors_from_body <- all(car_data$Doors == 4 - 2 * (car_data$convertible + car_data$coupe))
```
:::


`Doors` is redundant as well. Every convertible and coupe has two doors and
every other car four, so $\texttt{Doors} = 4 - 2\left(\texttt{convertible} + \texttt{coupe}\right)$
for every car (`doors_from_body` is TRUE), and with the body
style indicators in the model `Doors` would be an exact linear combination of
other columns. It is dropped.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
features <- c("Mileage", "Cylinder", "Cruise", "Sound", "Leather",
              setdiff(make_names, "Saturn"), setdiff(body_names, "wagon"))
p <- length(features)
```
:::


That leaves $p = 14$ candidate features, and the largest model is

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i \stackrel{ind}{\sim} N\left(0, \sigma^2\right),$$

where

- $y_i$ is the response for car $i = 1, \ldots, n$, with $n = 804$: its
price or, as decided next, the logarithm of its price,
- $x_{ij}$ is the value of feature $j = 1, \ldots, p$ for car $i$, in the order
Mileage, Cylinder, Cruise, Sound, Leather, Buick, Cadillac, Chevy, Pontiac, Saab, convertible, coupe, hatchback, and sedan, and $x_i = \left(1, x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{ip}\right)$ is
row $i$ of the model matrix $\mathbf{X}$,
- $\beta_0, \ldots, \beta_p$ are the coefficients, and
- $\epsilon_i$ is the error, with variance $\sigma^2$.

A **subset** of the features is a smaller model of the same form with the
coefficients of the other features set to zero.

### Price scale

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cars <- car_data |>
  transmute(log_price = log(Price), across(all_of(features)))
full_dollars <- lm(Price ~ ., data = select(car_data, Price, all_of(features)))
full_log <- lm(log_price ~ ., data = cars)
spread_cor <- c(dollars = cor(abs(residuals(full_dollars)), fitted(full_dollars)),
                log = cor(abs(residuals(full_log)), fitted(full_log)))

residual_plot <- function(fit, x_label, y_label, scale_name) {
  ggplot(tibble(fitted = fitted(fit), residual = residuals(fit)),
         aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
    labs(x = x_label, y = y_label,
         title = paste("All", p, "features, price", scale_name))
}
residual_plots <- list(
  residual_plot(full_dollars, "Fitted price ($)", "Residual ($)", "in dollars") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()),
  residual_plot(full_log, "Fitted log price", "Residual (log scale)", "on the log scale"))
```
:::

:::

The tabs plot the residuals against the fitted values of the largest model,
fit by least squares once with price in dollars as the response and once with
its natural logarithm.

![](10-subset-selection_files/figure-html/residual-log-figure-1.png){width=672}

:::

In dollars the residuals fan out as the fitted price rises: the correlation
between the absolute residual and the fitted value is
0.56. On the log scale it is
0.11, close to the constant variance the model
assumes. Errors of similar size on the log scale are errors of similar
percentage in price, which matches prices that vary by a few thousand dollars
for a Saturn and by many thousands for a Cadillac. From here on the response
is $y_i = \log\left(\texttt{Price}_i\right)$. The largest model explains
$R^2 = 92.9\%$ of the variability in log price,
with $\hat\sigma = 0.1103$.

### Selection motives

The largest model fits well, so why use fewer features?

- **Interpretability.** A model with fewer features is easier to explain, and
each coefficient that is truly zero but estimated anyway adds noise to the
story the model tells.
- **Variance.** Least squares fitted values are $\hat y = \mathbf{H}y$ with
$\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$,
so $Var\left[\hat y\right] = \sigma^2\mathbf{H}\mathbf{H}^\top = \sigma^2\mathbf{H}$. Its
trace is $\sigma^2\,\text{tr}(\mathbf{H}) = \sigma^2(d + 1)$ for a model with
$d$ features and an intercept, so

  $$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Var\left[\hat y_i\right] = \frac{\sigma^2(d+1)}{n},$$

  where $d$ is the **number of features** in the model, its **size**, and
  $\text{tr}$ is the trace. In the
  [Cross-Validation](../05-resampling/10-cross-validation.qmd) lecture $d$ was
  the degree of a polynomial; a degree-$d$ polynomial has $d$ features, so the
  two meanings agree there. Every feature added raises the average variance of
  the fitted values by $\sigma^2/n$, whether or not its true coefficient is
  zero; it lowers the bias only if its coefficient is not zero. With
  $n = 804$ and $p = 14$ the cost is small here, and it grows as $p$
  approaches $n$.

- **Search.** Each feature is either in or out, so there are $2^p$ candidate
models, $2^{14} = 16,384$ for these cars.

## Best subset selection

The figure plots log price (on a dollar axis) against mileage, one panel per
make, the view of the data the models below will be drawn on.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
log_price_axis <- scale_y_log10(breaks = c(10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 60) * 1000,
                                labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))
log_base <- ggplot(car_data, aes(x = Mileage, y = Price)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey55", alpha = 0.5, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ make) +
  mileage_axis +
  log_price_axis +
  labs(x = "Mileage", y = "Price (log scale)", title = "modeldata::car_prices")
```
:::

:::


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](10-subset-selection_files/figure-html/log-base-figure-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


Within a make the cars form bands at different price levels, cars that
differ in engine size and in other unrecorded ways, and within a band price
falls with mileage.

### Algorithm

**Best subset selection** fits every subset:

1. Let $\mathcal{M}_0$ be the null model, with no features, which predicts
$\bar y$ for every car.
2. For $d = 1, \ldots, p$, fit all $\binom{p}{d}$ models with exactly $d$
features by least squares, and let $\mathcal{M}_d$ be the one with the
smallest RSS, equivalently the largest $R^2$.
3. Choose one model among $\mathcal{M}_0, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_p$ with an
estimate of the error on new data: $C_p$, BIC, adjusted $R^2$, or
cross-validation.

Here $\mathcal{M}_d$ is the best model of size $d$, and $RSS_d$ is its
residual sum of squares. Step 2 compares models of the same size, and for them
the training RSS is a fair comparison: each has the same number of
coefficients to fit with. Step 3 compares models of different sizes, which is
where training error fails. The number of models fit is
$\sum_{d=0}^p\binom{p}{d} = 2^p$.

### Fitting

`leaps::regsubsets()` carries out step 2. The argument `nvmax` is the largest
size to search.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
best_fit <- regsubsets(log_price ~ ., data = cars, nvmax = p, method = "exhaustive")
best_summary <- summary(best_fit)
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Feature-by-size inclusion matrix, without the intercept column.
best_which <- best_summary$which[, -1]
features_of <- function(which_matrix, d) colnames(which_matrix)[which_matrix[d, ]]
nested <- all(map_lgl(2:p, \(d) all(best_which[d - 1, ] <= best_which[d, ])))
entry_size <- apply(best_which, 2, \(included) min(which(included)))
entry_order <- names(sort(entry_size))

which_plot <- function(which_matrix, title) {
  as_tibble(which_matrix) |>
    mutate(d = row_number()) |>
    pivot_longer(-d, names_to = "feature", values_to = "included") |>
    mutate(feature = factor(feature, levels = rev(entry_order))) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = d, y = feature, fill = included)) +
    geom_tile(color = "grey70") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "white", `TRUE` = "grey20"),
                      labels = c("Out", "In")) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_len(p), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    labs(x = "Model size d", y = NULL, fill = NULL, title = title)
}
best_which_plot <- which_plot(best_which, "Best subset of each size, all cars")

show_sizes <- 1:4
fitted_plots <- map(show_sizes, \(d) {
  fit <- lm(reformulate(features_of(best_which, d), "log_price"), data = cars)
  log_base +
    geom_point(data = mutate(car_data, Price = exp(fitted(fit))),
               color = "#D55E00", shape = 4, size = 0.9) +
    labs(subtitle = paste0("Fitted values (crosses) of the best model with ", d,
                           if (d == 1) " feature: " else " features: ",
                           paste(features_of(best_which, d), collapse = " + ")))
})
```

### Training RSS

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
X <- model.matrix(log_price ~ ., data = cars)
y <- cars$log_price
tss <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
# RSS of all 2^p subsets; column 1 of X is the intercept.
all_subsets <- map(0:p, \(d) {
  sets <- if (d == 0) list(integer(0)) else combn(p, d, simplify = FALSE)
  tibble(d = d, rss = map_dbl(sets, \(s) sum(lm.fit(X[, c(1, s + 1), drop = FALSE], y)$residuals^2)))
}) |>
  list_rbind()
best_rss <- all_subsets |>
  group_by(d) |>
  summarize(rss = min(rss), .groups = "drop")
rss_decreasing <- all(diff(best_rss$rss) < 0)

rss_plot <- ggplot(all_subsets, aes(x = d, y = rss)) +
  # A fixed jitter seed for this one figure, so drawing it leaves the
  # chapter's random number stream (and every later result) unchanged.
  geom_point(color = "grey60", alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  geom_line(data = best_rss) +
  geom_point(data = best_rss, size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:p) +
  scale_y_continuous(sec.axis = sec_axis(~ 1 - . / tss, name = expression(R^2))) +
  labs(x = "Model size d", y = "Training RSS",
       title = paste("All", format(2^p, big.mark = ","), "subsets; best of each size in black"))
```
:::

:::

The figure plots the training RSS of all
16,384 subsets against their size, with
the best of each size, $RSS_d$, joined by the black line. $R^2 = 1 - RSS/TSS$
is a decreasing function of RSS, so the right axis reads off the same points
as $R^2$.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](10-subset-selection_files/figure-html/rss-figure-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


$RSS_d$ falls at every step, from $RSS_0 = TSS = 135.06$ to
89.11 at $d = 1$ and 9.60 at
$d = 14$ (`rss_decreasing` is TRUE). It cannot do otherwise.
Adding any feature to $\mathcal{M}_d$ gives a model of size $d + 1$ whose
least squares fit can match $\mathcal{M}_d$ by setting the new coefficient to
zero, so $RSS_{d+1} \le RSS_d$. The training RSS and $R^2$ therefore always
choose $d = p$. This is the argument the
[Cross-Validation](../05-resampling/10-cross-validation.qmd) lecture made for
polynomial degree: training error rewards every addition, whether or not it
will help predict new cars.

### Computational cost

The 16,384 least squares fits above
take a few seconds. The count doubles with each candidate feature: $2^{20}$
is about a million, $2^{30}$ about a billion, and $2^{40}$ about a trillion.
The size of the search has a statistical cost too. The
[Cross-Validation in Practice](../05-resampling/15-cv-in-practice.qmd) lecture
showed that the smallest of many noisy estimates tends to be optimistic, and
the more
subsets searched, the more likely one of them fits the noise in these
particular cars well.

## Stepwise selection

The figure shows the correlation between every pair of features and with log
price.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cor_cars <- cor(cars)
cor_labels <- c(log_price = "log(Price)")
display_name <- function(v) if_else(v %in% names(cor_labels), cor_labels[v], v)
cor_plot <- as_tibble(cor_cars, rownames = "row") |>
  pivot_longer(-row, names_to = "column", values_to = "r") |>
  mutate(row = factor(display_name(row), levels = display_name(names(cars))),
         column = factor(display_name(column), levels = rev(display_name(names(cars))))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = row, y = column, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), size = 2.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#0072B2", mid = "white", high = "#D55E00",
                       limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation", title = "modeldata::car_prices") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```
:::

:::


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](10-subset-selection_files/figure-html/correlation-figure-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


`Cylinder` and `Cadillac` are the two features most correlated with log
price, 0.58 and
0.58, and with each other,
0.53: Cadillacs mostly have eight
cylinders. `Saab` is negatively correlated with `Cylinder`,
-0.37, because every Saab has four
cylinders, and positively with log price. Features that overlap like this
can substitute for each other, which is where a search that adds or removes
one feature at a time can go astray.

### Forward stepwise

**Forward stepwise selection** grows one model:

1. Let $\mathcal{M}_0$ be the null model.
2. For $d = 0, \ldots, p - 1$, fit the $p - d$ models that add one feature to
$\mathcal{M}_d$, and let $\mathcal{M}_{d+1}$ be the one with the smallest RSS.
3. Choose one model among $\mathcal{M}_0, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_p$ as in best
subset selection.

The number of models fit is

$$1 + \sum_{d=0}^{p-1}(p - d) = 1 + \frac{p(p+1)}{2},$$

106 for $p = 14$, against
16,384 for best subset selection. Forward stepwise
needs only $d < n$ for each model it fits, so it can be used when $p \ge n$,
stopping at size $n - 1$.

### Backward stepwise

**Backward stepwise selection** shrinks one model:

1. Let $\mathcal{M}_p$ be the model with all $p$ features.
2. For $d = p, \ldots, 1$, fit the $d$ models that remove one feature from
$\mathcal{M}_d$, and let $\mathcal{M}_{d-1}$ be the one with the smallest RSS.
3. Choose one model among $\mathcal{M}_0, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_p$ as before.

It fits the same $1 + p(p+1)/2$ models, but it starts from the full least
squares fit, so it needs $n > p$.

Both are **greedy**: forward never removes a feature it has added, and
backward never restores one it has removed, so their models are nested by
construction. The best model of size $d$ need not contain the best model of
size $d - 1$, and when it does not, a stepwise path misses it.

### Path comparison


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
forward_fit <- regsubsets(log_price ~ ., data = cars, nvmax = p, method = "forward")
backward_fit <- regsubsets(log_price ~ ., data = cars, nvmax = p, method = "backward")
same_forward <- identical(summary(forward_fit)$which, best_summary$which)
same_backward <- identical(summary(backward_fit)$which, best_summary$which)
```
:::


On all 804 cars the three methods give identical models at every size
(`same_forward` is TRUE and `same_backward` is TRUE),
because the best models happen to be nested. That is a property of these
data, not of the methods.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
n_halves <- 200
methods <- c("exhaustive", "forward", "backward")
method_labels <- c(exhaustive = "Best subset", forward = "Forward", backward = "Backward")
halves <- map(seq_len(n_halves), \(r) {
  id <- sample(n, n / 2)
  fits <- map(methods, \(m) summary(regsubsets(log_price ~ ., data = cars[id, ],

  names(fits) <- methods
  list(id = id, fits = fits,
       differs = map(fits[-1], \(f) rowSums(f$which != fits$exhaustive$which) > 0))
})
share_forward <- mean(map_lgl(halves, \(h) any(h$differs$forward)))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Beyond this course
- **Branch and bound.** `regsubsets(method = "exhaustive")` does not fit all
$2^p$ subsets: it uses the fact that removing features can only raise the RSS
to rule out whole branches of subsets without fitting them, which makes exact
best subset search practical up to a few dozen features.
- **Hybrid and floating searches.** Stepwise variants that, after each
addition, consider removing a feature added earlier (or the reverse) recover
some of the models a purely greedy path misses.
- **Mixed-integer optimization.** Modern integer-programming solvers can find
best subsets for hundreds of features.
- **Other models.** The same three algorithms apply to logistic or Poisson
regression, with the deviance in place of the RSS.
:::

## Model size

All three methods leave the same decision: which of
$\mathcal{M}_0, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_p$ to use. In this chapter all 804 cars
are training data. None are held out as test data, as they are in the test
data workflow of the
[Cross-Validation in Practice](../05-resampling/15-cv-in-practice.qmd)
lecture, so every estimate of error below comes from the same cars that
choose the model.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = zoom_from:p) +
```

:::

:::

The figure plots the training MSE, $RSS_d/n$, of the best model of each size
from $d = 6$ to $p$, with a dashed line at the estimate of the
error variance $\sigma^2$ from the largest model,
$\hat\sigma^2 = RSS_p/(n - p - 1) = 0.01216$.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](10-subset-selection_files/figure-html/train-mse-figure-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The training MSE is below $\hat\sigma^2$ from $d = 10$ on, and
equals 0.01193 at $d = p$. A new car's log price
varies about its mean with variance $\sigma^2$, so no model's average squared
error on new responses can be below $\sigma^2$; the training MSE of the larger
models is below an estimate of it. The training error cannot choose the size.
There are two ways to estimate the error on new data instead: adjust the
training error for the size of the model, or estimate the error directly by
cross-validation.

### Training error optimism

Fix a least squares model with $d$ features, and imagine new responses
$y_i^0$ at the same feature values $x_i$, independent of $y$ with the same
distribution. Write $f_i = E\left[y_i\right]$. Since
$E\left[y_i^0 - f_i\right] = 0$ and $y_i^0$ is independent of $\hat y_i$,

$$E\left[\left(y_i^0 - \hat y_i\right)^2\right] = \sigma^2 + E\left[\left(\hat y_i - f_i\right)^2\right], \qquad E\left[\left(y_i - \hat y_i\right)^2\right] = \sigma^2 + E\left[\left(\hat y_i - f_i\right)^2\right] - 2\,Cov\left[y_i, \hat y_i\right].$$

The training residual is smaller because $\hat y_i$ was fit to $y_i$. With
$\hat y_i = \sum_j h_{ij}y_j$ and independent errors,
$Cov\left[y_i, \hat y_i\right] = h_{ii}\sigma^2$, and summing over $i$,

$$E\left[\sum_{i=1}^n\left(y_i^0 - \hat y_i\right)^2\right] = E\left[RSS\right] + 2\sigma^2\,\text{tr}(\mathbf{H}) = E\left[RSS\right] + 2(d+1)\sigma^2,$$

where $y_i^0$ is a new response at $x_i$, $f_i$ its mean, and $h_{ij}$ the
$(i, j)$ entry of the hat matrix $\mathbf{H}$. The training RSS underestimates
the error on new responses at the same $x_i$ by $2(d+1)\sigma^2$ on average,
an amount that grows with the size of the model. For the largest model of the
figure above, $2(p + 1)\hat\sigma^2/n = 0.00045$
lifts the training MSE of 0.01193 to
0.01239, above
$\hat\sigma^2$.

### Penalized criteria

Adding that penalty back gives

$$C_p = \frac{1}{n}\left(RSS + 2d\hat\sigma^2\right), \qquad \text{BIC} = \frac{1}{n}\left[RSS + \log(n)\,d\hat\sigma^2\right], \qquad \text{Adjusted } R^2 = 1 - \frac{RSS/(n - d - 1)}{TSS/(n - 1)},$$

where

- $RSS$ is the training residual sum of squares of the model and $d$ its
number of features,
- $\hat\sigma^2$ is an estimate of the error variance from the model with all
$p$ features, the same for every size, which keeps the larger models from
estimating their own (smaller) error variance,
- $TSS = \sum_{i=1}^n\left(y_i - \bar y\right)^2$ is the total sum of squares,
and
- $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The subscript $p$ in $C_p$ is Mallows'
historical name, not the number of features.

$C_p$ is $RSS/n$ plus the optimism above divided by $n$, with $2d$ in place of
$2(d+1)$; the difference, $2\hat\sigma^2/n$, is the same at every size and does
not change which size wins. If $\hat\sigma^2$ is unbiased for $\sigma^2$, then
for a model fixed in advance
$E\left[C_p\right] + 2\sigma^2/n = E\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(y_i^0 - \hat y_i\right)^2\right]$:
up to the constant $2\sigma^2/n$, $C_p$ estimates the average error on new
responses at the observed feature values $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. Choose the size
with the smallest $C_p$ or BIC, or the largest adjusted $R^2$.

The **AIC** and **BIC** come from the likelihood. With
$\epsilon_i \stackrel{ind}{\sim} N\left(0, \sigma^2\right)$ and $\sigma^2$ fixed
at $\hat\sigma^2$, the maximized log-likelihood is
$\log L = -\frac{n}{2}\log\left(2\pi\hat\sigma^2\right) - RSS/\left(2\hat\sigma^2\right)$, and

$$\text{AIC} = -2\log L + 2(d+1), \qquad \text{BIC} = -2\log L + \log(n)(d+1).$$

Multiplying by $\hat\sigma^2/n$ and dropping the terms that do not depend on
$d$, among them the intercept's share of each penalty ($2\hat\sigma^2/n$ in
the AIC), leaves $C_p$ and the BIC above, so for least squares with Gaussian errors
AIC and $C_p$ choose the same size.

Each criterion trades a drop in RSS against a penalty per feature. Going from
$\mathcal{M}_d$ to $\mathcal{M}_{d+1}$ lowers $C_p$ if
$\left(RSS_d - RSS_{d+1}\right)/\hat\sigma^2 > 2$ and lowers the BIC if it
exceeds $\log(n) = 6.69$. Adjusted $R^2$ rises if
$RSS_{d+1}/(n - d - 2) < RSS_d/(n - d - 1)$, which rearranges to

$$F = \frac{RSS_d - RSS_{d+1}}{RSS_{d+1}/(n - d - 2)} > 1,$$

the $F$-statistic of the multiple regression lecture for the added feature.
For $n > 7$, $\log(n) > 2$, so the BIC penalizes each feature more than $C_p$
and tends to choose smaller models; adjusted $R^2$, with a threshold of 1 and
the error variance of the larger model in the denominator, penalizes least.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rss <- best_summary$rss
sizes <- seq_len(p)
sigma2_hat <- sigma(full_log)^2
criteria <- tibble(d = sizes,
                   Cp = (rss + 2 * d * sigma2_hat) / n,
                   BIC = (rss + log(n) * d * sigma2_hat) / n,
                   adj_R2 = 1 - (rss / (n - d - 1)) / (tss / (n - 1)))
d_cp <- which.min(criteria$Cp)
d_bic <- which.min(criteria$BIC)
d_adj <- which.max(criteria$adj_R2)
```
:::


On the cars, with $\hat\sigma^2 = 0.01216$, $C_p$ chooses
$d = 12$, the BIC $d = 10$, and adjusted $R^2$ $d = 14$.
The derivation holds for a model fixed in advance; $\mathcal{M}_d$ was chosen
as the best of $\binom{p}{d}$ fits, so its RSS is lower than a fixed model's
would be, and all three criteria share some of the selection optimism of the
[Cross-Validation in Practice](../05-resampling/15-cv-in-practice.qmd)
lecture.

### Within-fold cross-validation

Cross-validation estimates the error of each size on new cars directly. The
rule of the [Cross-Validation](../05-resampling/10-cross-validation.qmd) and
[Cross-Validation in Practice](../05-resampling/15-cv-in-practice.qmd)
lectures applies: every data-dependent step of the fit is repeated inside each
fold, using only the training folds. Here step 2 of
best subset selection is a data-dependent step. Within fold $\ell$, the best
model of each size is found from the training folds and then used to predict
the validation fold, the held-out fold $\ell$. Running best subset selection
once on all 804 cars and cross-validating only the coefficients would let the
held-out cars help choose the features that predict them.

`regsubsets()` has no `predict()` method, so `predict_subset()` multiplies
the model matrix of new cars by the coefficients of the best model of size
`d`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
predict_subset <- function(fit, new_data, d) {
  b <- coef(fit, id = d)
  X_new <- model.matrix(log_price ~ ., data = new_data)
  drop(X_new[, names(b), drop = FALSE] %*% b)
}
cv_by_size <- function(data, fold) {
  sq_error <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(data), p)
  for (l in unique(fold)) {
    held_out <- fold == l
    # Best subset of every size, from the training folds only.
    fold_fit <- regsubsets(log_price ~ ., data = data[!held_out, ], nvmax = p)
    for (d in seq_len(p)) {
      sq_error[held_out, d] <- (data$log_price[held_out] -
                                  predict_subset(fold_fit, data[held_out, ], d))^2
    }
  }
  colMeans(sq_error)
}
n_folds <- 10
fold_cars <- sample(rep(seq_len(n_folds), length.out = n))
cv_mse <- cv_by_size(cars, fold_cars)
d_cv <- which.min(cv_mse)
```
:::


$\text{CV}_{(k)}(d)$, the $k$-fold estimate with $k = 10$, estimates
the test MSE of the procedure "fit the best model of size $d$", not of one
fixed set of features: the best model of a size can differ from fold to fold.
The number of folds $k$ is unrelated to the $K$ of KNN or the number of
classes $K$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

fold_differs <- map(seq_len(n_folds), \(l) {
  w <- summary(regsubsets(log_price ~ ., data = cars[fold_cars != l, ], nvmax = p))$which
  rowSums(w != best_summary$which) > 0
}) |>
  do.call(what = rbind)

# The chosen size over further random partitions into folds.
n_partitions <- 20
partition_sizes <- map_int(seq_len(n_partitions), \(r) {
  which.min(cv_by_size(cars, sample(rep(seq_len(n_folds), length.out = n))))
})
partition_counts <- count(tibble(d = partition_sizes), d)
```

sizes 1, 4, and 7. Cross-validation chooses

### Coefficients

The model drops Cruise, Sound, Chevy, and Pontiac. With a normal error on the log scale,
$e^{x_i\beta}$ is the median price, so $e^{\hat\beta_j}$ multiplies the median
price per unit of feature $j$, a change of $100\left(e^{\hat\beta_j} - 1\right)\%$.

- **Intercept.** $e^{\hat\beta_0}$ = \$8,225 is
the estimated median price when every feature is zero: no miles, no leather,
a wagon, a reference make, and zero cylinders. No car has zero cylinders, so
$\hat\beta_0$ only sets the level; the same car with four cylinders has
estimated median price $e^{\hat\beta_0 + 4\hat\beta_{\texttt{Cylinder}}}$ = \$17,341.
- **Reference make.** Because Chevy and Pontiac were dropped, their
cars share the intercept with Saturn: the reference make is now
Chevy, Pontiac, and Saturn together, and each retained make
coefficient (Buick, Cadillac, and Saab) compares that make with those three.
Dropping a dummy variable merges its level into the reference.
- **Mileage.** Each additional 10,000 miles multiplies the median price by
$e^{10000\,\hat\beta_{\texttt{Mileage}}} = 0.921$,
holding the other features fixed.
- **Other features.** Each additional pair of cylinders multiplies the
median price by $e^{2\hat\beta_{\texttt{Cylinder}}} = 1.452$,
and the body style coefficients compare each style with a wagon.

### Optimistic inference

`summary(selected)` reports standard errors and $p$-values as though these
10 features had been chosen before seeing the data. They were chosen
because they fit these cars well, which makes both optimistic for two
reasons.

- **Error variance.** The standard errors are proportional to the selected
model's $\hat\sigma$, which comes from $RSS_d$, the smallest of
1,001 residual sums of squares of size
$d = 10$. The smallest of many RSS values tends to be lower than the
RSS of a model fixed in advance, so $\hat\sigma$ tends to be too small. On the
cars the selected model has $\hat\sigma = 0.1108$
against 0.1103 for the largest model: with 804 cars
the search lowers $\hat\sigma$ only a little, and dropping
Cruise, Sound, Chevy, and Pontiac raises it by more.
- **Large $|t|$.** A feature enters because its estimated coefficient is large
relative to its standard error in these data, so its $|t|$ statistic is large
and its $p$-value small, whatever its true coefficient.

The simulation below keeps the features of the 804 cars but replaces log
price with independent normal noise with standard deviation
0.1103, so every true coefficient is zero. Each noise
data set goes through best subset selection with the size chosen by $C_p$,
and the selected model is refit with `lm()`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
n_noise <- 500
noise_sims <- map(seq_len(n_noise), \(r) {
  noise_cars <- mutate(cars, log_price = rnorm(n, 0, sigma(full_log)))
  s <- summary(regsubsets(log_price ~ ., data = noise_cars, nvmax = p))
  s2 <- sigma(lm(log_price ~ ., data = noise_cars))^2
  noise_tss <- sum((noise_cars$log_price - mean(noise_cars$log_price))^2)
  # Cp of sizes 0 to p; size 0 is the null model.
  d <- which.min((c(noise_tss, s$rss) + 2 * (0:p) * s2) / n) - 1
  kept <- if (d == 0) character(0) else colnames(s$which)[s$which[d, ]][-1]
  fit <- lm(reformulate(if (d == 0) "1" else kept, "log_price"), data = noise_cars)
  list(d = d, sigma2 = sigma(fit)^2,
       p_value = summary(fit)$coefficients[-1, "Pr(>|t|)"])
})
noise_any <- mean(map_dbl(noise_sims, "d") > 0)
noise_p <- unlist(map(noise_sims, "p_value"))
noise_small_p <- mean(noise_p < 0.05)
noise_sigma2_bias <- mean(map_dbl(noise_sims, "sigma2")) / sigma(full_log)^2 - 1
noise_plot <- ggplot(tibble(p_value = noise_p), aes(x = p_value)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0,
                 fill = "grey70", color = "grey30") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "p-value of a kept noise feature", y = "Density",
       title = paste(length(noise_p), "noise features kept by Cp in",
                     n_noise, "noise data sets"),
       caption = "Dashed line: the p-value of a feature chosen in advance is uniform.")
```

## Conclusion

Subset selection chooses which of $p$ candidate features a least squares
model uses. Best subset selection fits every subset, $2^p$ models, keeps the
one with the smallest RSS at each size $d$, and then chooses among sizes.
Forward and backward stepwise selection build a nested path by adding or
removing one feature at a time, fitting $1 + p(p+1)/2$ models; they are
greedy, so their model of a given size need not be the best one, and backward
selection requires $n > p$.

Within one size, the training RSS is a fair way to compare models. Across
sizes it is not: the RSS and $R^2$ always improve as features are added, so
they always choose the largest model. The training RSS underestimates the
error on new responses at the same feature values by $2(d+1)\sigma^2$ on
average, which $C_p$ (equivalent to AIC for Gaussian least squares) adds back,
up to a constant. The BIC charges $\log(n)$ per feature instead of 2 and
favors smaller models; adjusted $R^2$ charges least. Cross-validation
estimates the error on new observations, at new feature values, directly,
and because choosing the
best model of each size is part of the fit, that search must be repeated
inside every fold from the training folds only. Criteria and cross-validation
often disagree where the estimated error is flat.

A selected model is interpreted like any regression, with one addition:
dropping some dummy variables of a categorical explanatory variable merges
those levels into the reference. Its standard errors and $p$-values ignore
the selection and are optimistic: its $\hat\sigma$ comes from the smallest of
many RSS values, and its features were kept because their $|t|$ statistics
were large.

The next lecture, ridge regression, keeps all $p$ features and instead
shrinks their coefficients toward zero by penalizing their size, with the
amount of shrinkage chosen by cross-validation.
